name: Payammal Shatrughna Temple
deity: Shatrughna, youngest brother of Rama, worshipped as Shatrughnaswamy and revered as an embodiment of Vishnu's Sudarshana discus
period: Traditionally ancient; damaged in the Mysore invasions of the late 18th century and restored by the village
summary: In the quiet countryside south of Irinjalakuda, the small temple of Shatrughna at Payammal completes the Nalambalam pilgrimage — a village shrine to the youngest of Rama's brothers, seen as the Lord's own discus.

sections.history: Payammal is the last and smallest of the four Nalambalam temples. In tradition its image of Shatrughna — youngest of Dasharatha's four sons and twin of Lakshmana — was one of the four found in the sea and installed by the chieftain Vakkayil Kaimal, Shatrughna's being given to Payammal. Its later story is one of loss and recovery. The temple declined amid struggles between local powers and was damaged during the Mysore invasions under Tipu Sultan in the late 18th century; tradition holds that the original panchaloha image was hidden in the temple pond for safety and never found again. The people of the village restored the shrine, and a granite image of Shatrughna now stands in the sanctum.
sections.architecture: Payammal is a modest Kerala village temple, its square sanctum set within a walled precinct in rural surroundings. There is no great tower or grand hall; the shrine's character lies in its simplicity. Close by lies the temple pond, the very waters that tradition says hold the lost metal image to this day. Within, Shatrughna stands in the granite image installed after the temple's restoration, honoured with the daily worship of a Vishnu shrine in the Kerala manner.
sections.legends: Shatrughna is revered here as an incarnation of the Sudarshana chakra, the blazing discus of Vishnu. His name means 'slayer of enemies', and devotees come to him to overcome adversity. The chief offering is the Sudarshana Pushpanjali, a flower worship made for victory over enemies and for prosperity, and some devotees offer a small Sudarshana chakra itself. It is also believed that the pilgrim should, where possible, attend the night puja here, to receive the Lord's protection in full.
sections.festivals: The temple's annual festival begins on the Pooyam asterism in Kumbham (February–March) and runs for five days. Its busiest season, though, is Karkidakam (July–August), when Nalambalam pilgrims arrive to complete their round with Shatrughna, many hurrying to finish all four temples before midday. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: After the crowds of Triprayar and Irinjalakuda, Payammal feels like a homecoming — a small shrine on a quiet village road where the Nalambalam pilgrimage comes gently to rest. In Karkidakam the lanes fill with buses and families completing the round; outside that season the temple is peaceful, and its simple courtyard invites a few minutes of stillness before the journey home.

visit.timings: Open in the early morning and again in the evening, with longer hours during Karkidakam for Nalambalam pilgrims. Confirm timings locally.
visit.dressCode: Traditional Kerala temple dress applies: men wear a mundu (dhoti) and remove their shirts before entering; women wear a saree, set-mundu or churidar. Entry is generally reserved for Hindus, per Kerala custom.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the temple; the outer surroundings may be photographed.
visit.gettingThere: Payammal is about 5 km south of Irinjalakuda in Thrissur district: turn off the Irinjalakuda–Kodungallur road at Arippalam and continue about 2 km. Irinjalakuda railway station, at Kallettumkara, is the nearest railhead, and Kochi international airport is roughly 40 km away by road. Nalambalam pilgrims usually arrive here last, after Moozhikkulam.
